title: Taxila’s hidden past
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
A HILL dismissed more than a century ago as an unremarkable heap of ruins has yielded one of Taxila’s most intriguing archaeological finds. Excavations at Jandial, led by Italian archaeologists, have exposed a structure nearly 100m long and more than 50m wide. It is located on an ancient road from Jandial’s Greek-style Ionic temple, outside the walls of the ancient city of Sirkap. Was it a place of worship, a public building or part of a larger complex? No one yet knows. That uncertainty is precisely what makes the discovery exciting. Taxila was a meeting place of peoples, beliefs, and architectural traditions, and the newly discovered remains could help explain how its communities organised their lives beyond the city walls. The finding follows last year’s discoveries at Bhir Mound, which raised fresh questions about how early urban life developed in the region. Together, they suggest that present accounts of Taxila still leave much unexplored.
The immediate priority should be properly funded research rather than grand claims about what has been found. Archaeologists need time to establish the monument’s age, purpose, and relationship with neighbouring sites. Their findings, including plans, photographs, and scientific assessments, should be made accessible to researchers and the public. Authorities must also protect the surrounding ground from construction and encroachment before potential evidence disappears. This is especially important given Unesco’s concerns earlier this year that restoration work at Mohra Moradu and Sirkap had compromised the authenticity of their ancient remains. The lesson is relevant to Jandial: excavation without careful preservation can destroy as much knowledge as it reveals. Pakistan should welcome the Italian partnership while investing in local archaeologists, conservation specialists and students who can continue the work. The greatest reward from Jandial will be a fuller, more accurate account of the varied civilisations that once shared this land.
Published in Dawn, October 13th, 2026

title: Politics or ‘war’?
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
OCTOBER has been most cruel to our fragile democracy. It has seen Liaquat Ali’s unresolved murder, 1954’s emergency, 1955’s One Unit move, Suhrawardy’s 1957 ouster, the 1958 and 1999 coups, governor’s rule in Sindh, and emergency/governor’s rule in KP now. This grim record reveals a deep malaise: broken institutions unable to resolve conflicts via reason and compromise, letting coercion fill the void. But no civilian era may have seen them as broken, biased and besmirched as now. A parliament born with a murky mandate has grown up to author partisan laws and fuel conflicts. Courts are seen as partisan players, not reliable referees. The executive uses one gear against dissent — force —true to its hybrid DNA.
The contrast could not have been starker as the centre’s maximal rigidity faced the PTI’s minimal demands. The centre’s misrule and disputed mandate justify peaceful protests on much bigger demands across South Asia recently: freshpolls, free courts, human rights, and the economy. But the PTI only sought the mild relief that the courts had given their leader Imran Khan on meetings and medical care. The centre reacted to even these timid asks with threats of emergency rule which has now been imposed.
It wanted the PTI to back a harsh Afg­han eviction policy. But evicting Afghans in need of refuge from the Afghan Taliban’s sins is hardly fair. Some may qualify for nationality and many contribute capital and labour, replacing millions of us now abroad. We must, instead, sympathise with ordinary Afghans as both of us are the worst victims of the sins of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. Mistreating them may boost our common foe. At the moment, ordinary Afghans here, far away from TTP training camps abroad, seem unlikely recruits. But harsh evictions may change both access and motive for some.
The centre blames PTI for the failure to end KP terrorism. But the centre also notes that terrorists cross borders, thus indicating that the primary responsibility lies with itself. Inland too, federal forces flex bigger muscles than the KP Police. So, the responsibility must be shared. Also, any large operation may again displace locals and most KP parties oppose it. Intelligence-led commando action closely coordinated with locals seems more suitable both tactically and morally. Islamabad should have accepted these ground realities.
The twin actions in KP will not help the centre.
Given the minimalist demands and these policy nuances, the twin KP actions in the midst of talks and a slow-motion march seem harsh. There are many PTI faults but also reasons for them being rooted in the party’s repression since 2023. The centre has bigger faults and fewer excuses. It should have first fixed its own shortcomings to convince the PTI to fix its faults and then forged a joint anti-terrorism strategy. Instead, it seems bent on a winner-takes-all war, not win-win politics with rivals. Force has replaced laws, norms, reason, compromise and decency as its default tool. This aspect has taken many past conflicts from institutions to the streets, where the state prevails easily, and then to the bush, where it struggles to end even those that lack popular and moral roots.
The twin actions in KP will not help the centre in either politics or security. Emergency rule may hand it administrative control in KP but not political authority. It may have tamed a hostile set-up but has also inflamed its voters. The vast power this regime has amassed has not translated into delivery, and is even less unlikely to do so in a troubled KP with an ad hoc, unpopular set-up. So, the PTI may gain politically as intensified repression helps it develop a victimhood narrative.
Defeating terrorism needs both public support and arsenal. Emergency and governor’s rule in KP may erode support to levels no arsenal can compensate for. The key drivers of terrorism may persist too. TTP camps may survive cross-border bombing. Porous borders will persist despite harsh travel and trade bans if federal policing remains weak.
The humility in a hybrid centre to adopt a terrorism policy that combines force with local wisdom and support may remain absent. It will gain an obedient KP junior partner, but one with weak support, legitimacy, and capacity. It has had such partners for decades in Balochistan, and yet terrorism persists there. KP may meet the same fate. The centre’s obsession with force may feed terrorism more than fight it.
The writer has a PhD degree from the University of California, Berkeley, in political economy and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

title: Busting the myths
author: none@none.com (Nazir A. Jogezai)
content:
INTELLECTUAL and wealthy Baloch are often a surprise for people in other parts of Pakistan. All preconceived notions stem from the stereotypical portrayals of the people of this vast province. As a result, the education, etiquette, intellect, and values of tolerance of the people of Balochistan are taken lightly.
A classmate of mine was, as I recall, introduced at one of Pakistan’s elite universities, with particular emphasis not on her qualifications but on the remote area in Balochistan to which she belonged. She felt that she had been singled out. Another aspect is grouping Balochistan’s applicants for jobs with under-represented categories, which shows a general reluctance to mainstream them. Special concessions — including a higher age limit — introduced to expand job opportunities in Balochistan also reinforce a sense of marginalisation. For example, when someone who holds an MPhil degree is accepted in a position that requires a PhD degree, it implies that candidates from Balochistan are not expected to compete on an equal footing with the others.
All this is due to the lack of knowledge about the geography, history, heritage, cultural and linguistic diversity of this land. Balochistan has valuable natural resources as well as the values of love, tolerance, openness, coexistence, and acumen. But, its cultural wealth has not been understood. Moreover, around seven different languages are spoken across the province. These represent seven distinct identities, each with its own cultural norms, values, and legacy. This diverse linguistic landscape is a true example of coexistence.
Despite deprivation, harsh sociopolitical conditions, a frail infrastructure, and serious security concerns, the Baloch people remain remarkably open-minded, intellectually charged, and socially aware. Indeed, their outlook and knowledge can match, and even surpass, that of people in the more developed parts of the country. Misconceptions have more to do with the lack of information about them. An analysis of formal education — educational institutions and curricula — and public awareness platforms, such as media and political discourse, often do not do justice to this region. Syllabi and textbooks also fail to inform the public. A more inclusive and balanced understanding of the province’s strengths and challenges must become a part of formal education, including through curricula and textbooks, educational policies and plans, and educational governance systems.
A deeper, more nuanced understanding of the Baloch is essential.
However, Balochistan should not be represented in the curriculum through the lens of deprivation. Prospectuses should integrate local languages, histories, literature, oral traditions, indigenous knowledge, and contemporary achievements alongside high-quality scientific and professional education — enabling students to view their heritage not as a marker of marginality but as a source of knowledge, identity, and possibility. Academic policies need to also be framed around the intellectual, cultural, and human resources within the province.
The media must not sensationalise the province’s sense of deprivation, reduce its people to tales of backwardness, or exploit their grievances for political or commercial purposes. Instead, it should present an accurate, nuanced image of Balochistan, extensively cover the issues its people face, and remain attentive to the province’s historical, social, and political context. In this way, the media can contribute to a more informed nat­ional understa­nding, which is always more be­­­neficial than reinforcing stereotypes and de­­­epening grievances.
The political elite must not view marginalisation as a po­­litically viable resource, or allow dependency and criticism to persist in order to consolidate its authority. Instead, they need to remain connected and work collectively to address the underlying challenges of the province. Meaningful political engagement requires accessibility and inclusion. Many political events, such as all-party conferences, are held in the federal capital, making them financially inaccessible to representatives of side-lined communities, and thereby limiting their participation in the national political discourse.
Ultimately, positive narratives are essential not only to address deprivation but also to reveal the true wealth of Balochistan, ie, its people, who are as capable, valuable, and deserving of recognition as any other citizen elsewhere in the country. Above all, such efforts can help overcome the persistent ‘curse’ which obscures their real identity, tolerance, capacity for coexistence, and intellectual potential. This vast and ancient land has to be celebrated for the strength and inclusive values of its people.
The writer is an educationist.

title: Import fraud
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE under-invoicing of imports from China is not an allegation. It is an open secret in Pakistan’s markets — one that has been known for years. The gap between imports recorded from China and what China itself reports exporting is estimated to be in the range of $3.5-5bn in any single year. The Faisalabad loom owners have described this practice as one of the reasons their business is suffering. Yarn and cloth are the visible case, but the practice runs through the entire import trade from China — from machinery parts and chemicals to electronics, tyres, and household goods. Traders declare a fraction of the true value, pay duty and sales tax on that fraction, and sell at prices no domestic competitor can match. It could not happen at this scale without Customs. Valuation is checked at the port. When the same understatement recurs across the same products, importers, clearing agents, and officers who pass the consignments, year after year, it points past carelessness to facilitation.
The damage is easy to trace. The exchequer loses duty and tax every day. Local manufacturers are forced to compete against goods whose prices have been shaved by a pen stroke. Mills close, looms are sold, workers go home. Then the same industry is told to become competitive and increase exports. It cannot, while its home market is being undercut by tax evasion that the state declines to acknowledge. It also corrupts what the country knows about itself. Imports are undercounted, so the trade deficit and the revenue gap are misstated, and policy is built on wrong numbers. The tools are already in place. Pakistan and China operate an electronic data exchange between their Customs administrations, and Islamabad has asked Beijing for real-time data. Applied to every shipment, not just textiles, comparing the Chinese export declaration with the Pakistani goods declaration would show mismatches in value and quantity at once. Large gaps should mean investigation, penalties, and prosecution. It is an argument for collecting what the law already requires, from everyone, equally. Cheaper power and easier credit mean little to a producer who is underpriced at the border. The government has assured the loom owners that their problems will be resolved. Controlling under-invoicing at the Pakistan-China border should be a good start.
Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

title: Tax game
author: none@none.com (Farooq Arby)
content:
FOR decades, the FBR has found itself stuck in a loop of introducing a series of simplified schemes to bring the vast informal sector into the tax net, only to watch them fall flat. The latest initiative, the Fixed Tax Asaan Scheme for traders, offered a simplified filing process, a flat one per cent tax on turnover, and immunity from routine audits. Yet, despite targeting an estimated 3.5 million eligible traders, only a few thousand enrolled, generating a negligible amount of tax against a target of Rs50 billion.
To understand why well-intentioned schemes consistently fail, we must look beyond administrative sprints and examine the dynamics between taxpayers and the tax collector. In a strategic environment, players choose their actions based on expected payoffs. An analysis of the tax system under a game-theoretic framework, pioneered in Pakistan by renowned economist Dr Hafiz Pasha, helps explain how taxpayers develop strategies to counter the efforts of tax authorities.
Consider, for example, the distinction between filers and non-filers, introduced to encourage greater formality. In essence, it is a weak policy lever: it penalises not being on the Active Taxpayers List rather than concealing income. An individual facing this distinction has three broad strategies: file honestly, file a return declaring nil or very little taxable income, or remain outside the tax system altogether. Honest filing can be the costliest option because it exposes income and assets to greater tax scrutiny. Staying outside the system, meanwhile, attracts higher tax rates on transactions such as property and vehicle purchases and certain financial transactions. The third option of filing with minimal declared income may be the cheapest route. Given the perception of FBR’s limited enforcement capacity, it may be a preferred strategy.
Interestingly, the evidence also supports this. Income tax return filing has risen sharply, from around 2m returns in 2018 to about 6m now. Yet tax payments associated with return filing have not always kept pace with the growth in the number of filers.
Traders are smarter than the FBR. This should be recognised.
Similar is the case with the recent Tax Asaan Scheme for traders. The FBR attempted to break the informality trap through incentives. By reducing compliance costs and offering audit protection, alongside a green plate as a visible identifier for compliant businesses, the scheme sought to lower barriers to entry and make participation in the formal economy safer and mutually beneficial. However, despite these incentives, the FBR has failed to establish a cooperative equilibrium.
Traders responded poorly to the scheme, which is an important lesson: making compliance cheaper and easier does not automatically make it attractive. A trader faces two choices. The first is to enter the tax system, declare turnover, pay tax, and establish a documented financial identity. The second is to remain outside the system. If staying outside carries little expected cost, the latter may still offer the greater payoff.
Traders are smarter than the FBR. This should be recognised. The FBR plays within fixed parameters, while taxpayers have many more ways to adjust their strategies and work around them. Moreover, the FBR may be myopic, driven by the immediate pressure to meet revenue targets, while businesses consider a much longer time horizon.
Perhaps the most serious issue with the design of this scheme is its time horizon. Traders have concerns ab­o­ut the next round of the game. They do not view tax compliance as a one-off decision; they evaluate it as a repeated game. Their primary concern may not be the paperwork req­u­ired today, but the longer-term implications of documentation. They fear that disclosing the true scale of their businesses now could enable the government to change the rules in future rounds, requiring them to account for their sources of wealth, personal assets, and expenditure. They have legitimate concerns about policy continuity: will the 1pc tax rate remain unchanged? Will audit exemptions continue? Could the information disclosed today later be used for broader tax assessments?
If the FBR wants a genuinely cooperative equilibrium, it must move beyond ad hoc, short-term schemes and focus on restructuring the underlying payoffs. It should prioritise meaningful tax reforms over the pursuit of immediate revenue targets, with greater emphasis on policy stability and predictability. Taxpayers must be given credible assurance that the rules will not later be changed in ways that penalise those who voluntarily enter the formal system.
The writer is an economist.

title: Paralysed prisons
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S overcrowded jails distort the intention of imprisonment — rehabilitation, education, and occupational development. The Annual Prisons Data Report 2026, compiled by the National Commission for Human Rights and Justice Project Pakistan, reveals that attention to lengthy confinement, delays in trials, and difficulties in obtaining bail has been long overdue. It also finds that Pakistan’s jails, built for 68,832 people, were operating at over 160pc of their capacity. The prison system currently holds 41,681 more people. As a result, 110,513 are packed in tight, squalid spaces. Three out of every four inmates are caught in legal paralysis and are awaiting trial. Punjab and Sindh have witnessed a substantial rise in inmate numbers, with prisons in KP and Balochistan still operating within capacity.
That the prison system is fractured is no surprise. Dismal sanitation, malnutrition, absent healthcare, and overcrowding define it. Not only are inmates compelled to devise sleeping rosters, they also face mental health hazards. Those with psychosocial debilities face endless jail time and abuse without medical care. Troublingly, the number of women in jail is on the rise. Since 2024, their numbers have gone up by 46pc; a number of children, too, await trial. These conditions illustrate how easily citizens are deprived of civil freedoms. For decades, there has been little meaningful change. The crisis is worsened by overreliance on custodial measures. While the various initiatives to improve the jail infrastructure must be appreciated, an overhaul in the bail and surety processes, along with speedy trials, can actually reduce the under-trial population. Meanwhile, serious health concerns are widespread, with reports of cases of hepatitis, HIV, and diabetes. Insight into how individual conditions — such as mental health issues and drug addiction — worsen without treatment is the hallmark of a system that cares for its people, prisoners included.

title: Perilous misstep
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE federal government on Sunday made good on its threat to dismiss an elected government and impose governor’s rule and emergency in KP. The president obliged. The head of state, the only civilian elected twice to that office, has now imposed governor’s rule three times: Punjab in 2009, Balochistan in 2013, and now KP — though the ruling PML-N is the main driver behind the latest move. His party, the PPP, has done so six times in the short history of Pakistani democracy, the others being in 1973 (Balochistan), 1975 (the then NWFP), and 1994 (again, KP). There is, therefore, nothing novel about Sunday’s move. However, it is a measure that has never achieved what its authors intended, and has more often than not backfired. That, perhaps, is why even those unsympathetic to the PTI government in Peshawar had been warning Islamabad not to take this step. In going ahead with it, the centre assumes responsibility for any blowback.
The imposition of governor’s rule in Balochistan in 1973 is instructive. In February of that year, the then prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto dismissed the Balochistan government led by Sardar Attaullah Mengal, and also removed the then governor, Mir Ghaus Bakhsh Bizenjo. The centre ruled directly through Nawab Akbar Khan Bugti and sent in the army, fuelling an already smouldering insurgency. Many elected Baloch leaders turned separatist. The province never really recovered. KP is not Balochistan, and the PTI is no separatist movement. But the parallel of an elected leadership being swept aside on the pretext of security is unmistakable. The experience of the 1973 decision should be seen as a warning that this is how estrangement from the federation begins.
There is no political justification for governor’s rule. If the authorities felt terrorism was increasing in some tribal districts and adjoining areas, they could have limited themselves to imposing a targeted emergency under Article 232, as they have already done. To deprive an entire province of its elected government is not only undemocratic; it can also be severely counterproductive, as history shows. The stated reason for Sunday’s decision is terrorism. The real target is perceived to be the only provincial government the opposition held, and the agitation it was leading. The PTI government may have faltered on several fronts, but in a democratic society, those failings are supposed to be addressed through the electoral process, not through executive fiat. Under Article 234, the proclamation lapses within two months unless parliament approves it. That is where this ill-considered action should be challenged on principle: lawmakers would do well to scrutinise it, and the courts to test whether the constitutional threshold was actually met. Islamabad must extricate itself from this quagmire before it deepens, and leave KP’s governance to those its people have elected to oversee it.
Published in Dawn, October 12th, 2026

whyMatters: This article offers a critical analysis of the imposition of governor's rule, a recurring constitutional and political challenge in Pakistan. For competitive exams, it provides crucial arguments, historical precedents, and constitutional references relevant to questions on federalism, democratic stability, and civil-military relations.
summary: The federal government imposed governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), an act with numerous historical precedents in Pakistan.
The article argues that such measures have consistently failed to achieve their intended objectives and have often backfired, leading to greater estrangement and instability.

It contends that there is no political justification for imposing governor's rule across an entire province, suggesting that a targeted emergency under Article 232 would be sufficient for security concerns.
The editorial views this as an undemocratic move targeting an opposition-led provincial government, urging parliament and courts to challenge its constitutional validity under Article 234.
facts: The President, as the only civilian elected twice, has now imposed governor's rule three times: Punjab (2009), Balochistan (2013), and KP (latest).
The PPP has imposed governor's rule six times in Pakistan's history (1973 Balochistan, 1975 NWFP, 1994 KP, 2009 Punjab, 2013 Balochistan, and the latest in KP).
The imposition of governor's rule in Balochistan in 1973 led to a fuelled insurgency and many elected leaders turning separatist, resulting in long-term provincial estrangement.
Under Article 234 of the Constitution, a proclamation of governor's rule lapses within two months unless approved by parliament.

Article 232 of the Constitution of Pakistan (Proclamation of Emergency on account of War, Internal Disturbance, etc.)

title: Rebuilding values
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
AT a time when good news is scarce, it was gratifying to see Navanethem ‘Navi’ Pillay receive the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. Pillay is a South African judge at the International Court of Justice and former UN high commissioner for human rights. She chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Such symbolic support for justice, human rights, and international law has been much wanting in recent years.
Sadly, Pillay’s prize can also be perceived as a eulogy for international rule of law, which has been flagrantly disregarded, particularly in conflict contexts — from the targeting of civilian infrastructure to the use of chemical weapons and genocidal acts. As if to ring the death knell of the rules-based order, hours after Pillay received the honour, the US sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), a punitive measure that would make it impossible for the court to function.
That we now inhabit a multipolar, post-liberal democratic world order is evident. But moments like these highlight the extent to which the world we’ve known has been torn asunder. The collapse of liberal democratic norms leaves a vacuum which countries must now consider how to fill. This is not all bad — liberal democratic frameworks had imperial overtones, prioritised unfettered economic growth at the expense of social welfare and the planet, and engendered hypocrisy because those touting them were often unlikely to abide by them. But what has come in their wake is authoritarianism and a hyper-privileging of national sovereignty of the kind that enables the US — never a member state of the ICC — to declare the court a “rogue” institution. With World Values Day looming this Thursday, the question to ask is whether countries will use the world order vacuum to refresh national values in this era of national sovereignty.
The speed of developments in these uncertain times means that nations rarely get time to reflect or publicly debate before taking decisions in a way that allows for alignment with national values or sovereign principles. With each destabilising development, whether invasions, pandemics or natural disasters, realpolitik reigns.
National values that work for all must emerge organically.
Today’s conflict and energy dynamics lead to expedient defence pacts, the pervasiveness of AI forces countries to sign up to global technology governance frameworks, and the stop-start flow of climate finance leads nations to make ambitious climate commitments. Little heed is paid to whether these policy decisions cohere and complement or contradict and undermine each other.
In recent decades, the onus to cohere was less; the liberal democratic framework, with all its flaws and flows of money, offered some coherence — rule of law, rights, justice, but also individualism and rampant capitalist growth. But in its absence, the centre will not hold. This is why an intentional revisiting of national values may be welcome. The idea may cause shudders. National values in recent memory have been the bogeymen of authoritarians and dictators, imposed from the top down. Think of nations that have doubled down on alternative value systems, and places like Afghanistan and North Korea come to mind.
National values that work for all must emerge organically from tradition, practice, a nuanced understanding of history and a desire to progressively engage with national documents such as constitutions. They must be inclusive, dynamic and open to challenge, and reflected across policy, law, and curricula. The best values are the products of difficult reckonings — truth and reconciliation proceedings, high-profile trials. This is a tall order for states like Pak­istan that are ‘takers’ of political sta­nces, standards, and policies.
Ironically, it seems as if the thi­ng that will replace the coherence of the liberal democratic world order will be AI’s rampaging monoculture. As all knowledge production, financial systems, and policymaking draw from the same well of AI slop, a consistency will emerge from the omnipresence of Big Tech and LLMs. Don’t ask me what that will look like.
Instead, let’s look at an example of what values emerge when all state structures, humanitarian norms and justice are stripped away. The horrific and hugely underreported conflict in Sudan has led to the emergence of the country’s Emergency Response Rooms, strong Nobel Peace Prize contenders alongside Pillay. These are among the few sources of relief in Sudan, offering food, healthcare, schooling, counselling, and protection. These organisations are staffed by 26,000 volunteers and have grown from community kitchens and pandemic-era clinics into the primary solace from the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. Perhaps a return to the most basic values is the best way forward.
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.

title: Why stability is elusive
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
RECENT events are another reminder of how elusive political stability remains in the country. The confrontation between PTI and the government escalated after an effort at dialogue between them ended in mutual recriminations. PTI pressed ahead with its protest march that the federal government tried to stop by threatening to oust the KP government through imposition of governor’s rule. The usual wave of arrests of party activists preceded the opposition’s march. The Shehbaz Sharif government is now set on imposing an emergency and governor’s rule in KP in a move that is likely to inflame sentiment in the province and exacerbate the situation.
This is a rerun of a familiar script, except it is set against a backdrop of deepening authoritarianism. It also marks a dangerous phase in confrontational politics with the federal authorities and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government at loggerheads. Inflammatory rhetoric by federal ministers was matched by fiery speeches from KP’s Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.
Other than the brief interlude of dialogue, the government responded to the opposition protest by its usual mix of coercion, threats, and incendiary statements. It took the consequential decision to impose an emergency in KP and bring the province under federal control. The cabinet has approved this while parliament has been convened to sanction the move. The most egregious use of coercion was the reported abductions and incommunicado detention of over eight PTI MPs, including three members of the National Assembly. Using coercive means to manage the opposition has only reinforced the government’s slide into authoritarianism, which has resulted in the country’s democratic decline. This has been evidenced in the past couple of years in actions taken against the opposition and other critics:banning public gatherings, breaking up protest demonstrations, arresting opposition supporters, raiding homes of political leaders, filing cases against them, policing the media, imposing internet restrictions and criminalising free speech. Another telling indicator of democratic regression is the undermining of judicial independence by controversial amendments and defiance of court orders. The erosion of institutions meant to check executive power has contributed to growing autocratisation. The shell of democracy remains, but it is increasingly hollowed out.
The aim of these actions is to tighten the government’s grip on the political system and the country. But it does not make the government strong. It signals weakness, not confidence. Some argue there is nothing new in this phase of repression, that it continues a familiar tradition and borrows from a well-worn playbook. Previous civilian governments, too, were guilty of undemocratic conduct, intolerance of opposition, jailing rivals on trumped-up charges, marginalising parliament, curbing press freedom, and undermining judicial independence. All of this is true. But the scale and scope of the repressive measures today go beyond anything seen under a civilian government before.
Using coercive measures and undermining institutions do not produce stability.
Public space is being encroached upon in an unprecedented manner. Because there is more to control in the digital era, especially social media, the present government has gone much further than its civilian predecessors in imposing digital space curbs and censorship and micromanaging the electronic media.
The rationale offered by spokesmen of the hybrid government, when pressed to justify such measures, is that they are necessary for political stability. But does the veneer of calm imposed by force bring stability? On the contrary, it is a recipe for instability. Coercion does not produce stability. It deepens polarisation, erodes the social contract, divides the country further, and fuels uncertainty. The opposition represents a large section of society, has a significant parliamentary presence, and runs the government in KP. To suppress and demonise it does not promote stability. It guarantees the continuation of political confrontation.
The economic cost of relentless political tensions and government-opposition conflict is plain to see. Frequent shutdowns and blockade of cities hit businesses hard. It vitiates the business climate. This at a time when recovery has yet to take hold, economic growth remains anaemic and stabilisation is still fragile. Jittery investors hold back, deterred by the spectre of turmoil and unrest. Celebrating every tranche received from the IMF doesn’t obscure the reality that the economy is yet to embark on the path to sustainable growth. Meanwhile, all recent surveys — Gallup, Ipsos — show declining public confidence in economic conditions and pessimism about the country’s economic future. Clearly, the country’s economic problems cannot be tackled in a politically volatile environment.
Political stability requires a reset on several fronts. It needs the creation of a peaceful and predictable political environment resting on a truce and mutual accommodation between the government and opposition. A divided and polarised country cannot be stable. Genuine dialogue is needed that is aimed at a lasting modus vivendi, not driven by short-term expediency to stop the next protest march. It also means the government relenting in its inhumane treatment of PTI leader Imran Khan in defiance of court orders. The recent talks were doomed when the government wasn’t even willing to allow opposition leaders to meet Khan for consultations on the negotiations. It also remains unwilling to grant him his entitlement under the law. Such an attitude cannot form the basis for serious negotiations, let alone a political settlement.
Political stability is also achieved by governing the country inclusively by consensus and not by excluding other political actors who command substantial electoral and public support. A ‘winner-takes-all’ approach has long characterised Pakistan’s politics. This has rested on the mistaken assumption that the party that wins an election (almost always on a minority vote and, in the case of the present government, in a disputed poll) is the ‘sole representative’ of the people. This stance leads to inherently unstable and exclusionary governance. Unilateral rule not only erodes democracy; it also undermines effective governance. The country’s federal nature makes inclusive governance essential. The centre must work with and not against opposition-run provinces.
Political stability is also built by ensuring an environment where the rule of law prevails. It involves strengthening institutions and not weakening them in pursuit of ephemeral ‘control’. Strong institutions ensure predictability — the bedrock of stability. They provide the checks and balances that are essential to prevent the abuse of power and protect fundamental rights and civil liberties.
To those who believe stability can be achieved by ousting an elected provincial government, concentrating power and discarding democratic freedoms, Pakistan’s history stands testimony to how disastrous that path has been for the country and its people.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.

title: A theorist of crisis
author: none@none.com (Umair Javed)
content:
BORN in Karachi in 1945, Anwar Shaikh, a giant of Marxian economics and professor at The New School in New York, passed away last week. His father served in the Foreign Service as a result of which his family moved around frequently, through Malaysia, Canada, Kuwait, and finally the US. It was in Kuwait, he would later say in a biographical note from 2016, that economics first claimed him: standing amid the gleaming infrastructure of an oil economy, he could not reconcile the scale of wealth with the poverty of those who produced it. The obvious question was why. He spent the next half-century building an answer to this and its related questions.
I came to Shaikh’s work first through an undergraduate class: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar’s Political Economy of Development and Underdevelopment course, which featured Shaikh’s short four-page elaboration of Marx’s theory of exploitation published in a 1990 reader on Marxian economics compiled by Eatwell, Milgate, and Newman. It was only later on, after having joined academia myself, that I picked up a more sustained interest in his political economy contributions. Many of these were based on the workings of the advanced capitalist world, but to me it felt possible — via a universalist understanding of the capital-labour relation that characterises our shared modernity — that one could recover a broader insight and logic extendable to other contexts as well.
His magnum opus, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises, published by Oxford in 2016 after nearly 20 years of writing, is not an easy book. It runs into nearly 1,000 pages and I have only been able to digest parts of it, a process aided greatly (and almost singularly) by his video lectures on YouTube. However, its central propositions are clear enough to state plainly — capitalism is driven by the pursuit of profit as a structural consideration. Firms invest, hire, fire, pollute, underpay, and cut corners not out of some moral imperative or ethical inadequacies, but because competition demands it.
Competition, Shaikh insisted, is quite unlike the “decorous ballet” of textbook economics. It is a war, fought with prices, wages, lobbying, disinformation, and whatever else gives one firm an edge over another. In this universe, marked as it is by war, it’s a bit difficult to model markets as tending towards equilibrium (as orthodoxy usually claims). Shaikh, instead, argued that rather than any form of stasis, capitalism fluctuates, overshoots, crashes, recovers, and overshoots again.
What is worth celebrating in Anwar Shaikh’s work is his insistence that economics is never neutral.
Mainstream accounts tend to view these as ‘failures’ (of regulation or rationality). Someone like Shaikh, on the other hand, would see these as systemic features of a mode of production built on separating the producers of value from the means of production.
His writings on so-called externalities generated by this systemic feature of competition are worth dwelling on, given the cost-of-living and ecological crises plaguing the planet. Orthodox economics treats pollution, low wages, and dangerous working conditions as costs that firms impose on society from outside the market, ie, as unfortunate side effects, correctable with the right regulations.
Shaikh went as far as calling this view of externality a conceptual fraud. Rather than by accident, a firm pollutes because the alternative — investing in cleaner production — costs money that would otherwise be profit. The extraction and pollution are thus internal to how profit works. The same point has also been made at a more philosophical level by theorist Alysa Battistoni, who argues how nature is classified as a “free gift” under capitalism, ie, as something that does not carry with it the moral force of reciprocity or care (unlike a real gift).
Beyond the intricate debates with the mainstream, what is worth celebrating in Shaikh’s work is his insistence that economics is never neutral. In his own words, he asserted that “there is no such thing as a value-free or socially neutral economics”. Every model encodes assumptions about how society works and who it works for. The amnesty schemes, the short-lived consumption-led booms, the stabilisation programmes that periodically arrive with the IMF, the growth targets announced at press conferences, the optimistic narratives about investor confidence and trickle-down are all consequences of choices made in a particular direction and for particular interests.
Shaikh spent his career mapping those choices with a view to uncovering their systemic root in the unceasing motivation for profit. By implication, he ends up showing how reformist ‘tinkering’ that seeks to curtail externalities and fallouts is ultimately futile, and how a far more fundamental overhaul is required.
Shaikh was educated partly at St Patrick’s in Karachi, before finishing his schooling in New York, his undergraduate at Princeton, his doctoral studies at Columbia, and a long career of teaching and research at the New School for Social Research in New York. During that time, he was always on the heterodox edge of the discipline, and concerned with abstract theory, which explains why his work never found the same recognition in a society that otherwise rushes to embrace high-achievers with even the most ephemeral of connections to Pakistan.
However, that biography — from Karachi to a position of heterodox criticality in American academic life — carries a relevant resonance right now. In the face of geopolitical and economic reordering, the questions of whose economics we use, the viability of its long-held orthodoxies, and what they are actually deployed for, matter more urgently in Pakistan and the world at large than at any point in the recent past. It is then truly unfortunate that we have lost one of the clearest thinkers available on such questions.
The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.

title: The pushed river
author: none@none.com (Mushtaq Gaadi)
content:
THE Indus River is moving east in central Pakistan. Along an 85-kilometre stretch from upstream of Layyah city down to Taunsa Barrage, it is pressing hard against its eastern bank.
In this year’s flood season, it destroyed Basti Kanjal, a riverine settlement of more than 500 houses some 15km northwest of Layyah. It did not stop there, washing away several more settlements. Since June, close to 5,000 acres of cultivated land have been lost; according to news reports, 100,000 people have been displaced. A close analysis of 38 years of satellite imagery shows that the river is not wandering. It is being pushed.
Ask any elder in the riverside villages of Churkin or Basira which face the Vehowa hill torrent’s mouth 30km upstream of Layyah about the river of his childhood, and he will tell you the Indus was 10 miles (16km) wide. He will also tell you that the river gave as much as it took: land drowned on one bank surfaced on the other, and the patwari’s records followed the water back and forth. The satellites agree with him on the width. Between 1988 and 1997, the active belt below Churkin measured 16km to 18km, and above Taunsa Barrage nearly 24km. Today, it is reduced to a third. A river squeezed into a narrow gut runs deeper and faster, and expends its vigour on eroding vulnerable banks.
Three engineering structures, built with public money and international loans, have together hemmed in the river on three sides. The first of these is the Chashma Right Bank Canal, financed by the Asian Development Bank. The canal runs through the Suleiman hill torrents. These are no small streams: the Vehowa alone drains a catchment of over 2,600 square kilometres and has recorded flood peaks above 35,000 cusecs. Before the canal, such floods spread across the Daman plain under the old rod-kohi system, watering the land and dropping their silt on the way. After 2003, the canal’s 68 cross-drainage structures began delivering every flood, with its full load of mountain sediment, to fixed points on the river’s right bank. Between 2011 and 2016, two great fans of new land rose out of the riverbed — one at the Vehowa’s mouth opposite Layyah, and one at the mouth of the Sanghar torrent near Taunsa city. Together, they hold some 37sq km of new permanent land, a metre and more above the old riverbed, and about 100 million cubic metres of sediment. Where the trained torrents deliver their load, walls have risen; in the intervening stretches, the river’s western edge hasn’t moved in 38 years. The canal itself has been closed since the 2022 floods, but its silt walls remain standing in the river.
A close analysis of 38 years of satellite imagery shows that the Indus is not wandering. It is being pushed.
The second factor is Taunsa Barrage. Built in 1958 to pass a million cusecs, its capacity fell by half within five decades as sediment accumulated. A wedge of silt today stands nearly 2m high near the pond and stretches 40km upstream, flattening the river’s slope and promoting further deposition. The World Bank’s 2005-08 rehabilitation project raised the crest and built a secondary weir downstream. But the embankments were never raised proportionately. Local communities protested and wrote to the Bank that the remodelling ignored the sedimentation, causing flood protection for structures to fail. In 2010, a flood peak of 960,000 cusecs breached the eastern marginal embankment upstream, allowing the river to outflank the structure and carve a new channel. Their warning proved correct.
The third factor relates to the embankments. The marginal ones along the left bank, running some 40km from Daira Din Pannah up towards Layyah, froze the river’s eastern edge decades ago, and the floodplain strip between the river and bund has since been almost entirely converted into farms and settlements. In the 1990s, the river still reclaimed that strip in every high flood; today, 95 per cent of it has turned into permanent land. Meanwhile, the restricted riverbed is level with the protected villages outside — all that protects them now is the crest of an earthen bund.
This is the fuller picture of the narrative that those affected recounted outside the Layyah Press Club this September, as they blamed two decades of Chashma Canal silt for their plight: sediment walls advancing from the west, a wedge of silt backed up behind the barrage, and, on the east, the embankments holding the door shut. A river so enclosed has nowhere to go but against the weakest point. In 2010, the weakest point was the marginal bund above Taunsa; in 2026, it was the training works at the Layyah bridge. The river has now cut to within 200m of the Lala, its old channel passing along the western edge of Layyah city. The city’s protection bund stops 3.5km short of that point.
What happens if the river completes its eastward shift? The low floodplain east of the river holds hundreds of villages built on the assumption that the river would keep to its corridor. A river breaching the Lala line would place Layyah on the front line, and behind it Jaman Shah, Kot Sultan, and Paharpur. An eastward-shifted Indus would progressively outflank Taunsa Barrage itself. A barrage commands only the water that arrives at its gates; the canals of Dera Ghazi Khan and Muzaffargarh, irrigating millions of acres, depend on that command. The river would leave the barrage presiding over a dying channel.
    
The communities of this region warned both lending institutions years ago, the ADB over the canal and the World Bank over the barrage, through formal complaints, inspection claims, and hunger strikes. I was among those who warned. I remember how patiently they were heard and how completely they were ignored. Both institutions noted lessons and closed their files. The river has now reopened them, writing its supplement in drowned villages and 5,000 acres of lost land. Reconstruction without the benefit of an honest analysis of these structural challenges would be tantamount to allowing a similar situation, or even worse, in the future. The analysis now exists, measured from orbit and verifiable by anyone. What remains is whether anyone with authority is willing to read it.
The writer is a native of Taunsa and teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026
topic: River Management, Flooding, and Infrastructure Impact in Pakistan

summary: The Indus River, along an 85-kilometre stretch, is being 'pushed' eastwards, causing significant erosion, land loss (5,000 acres), and displacement (100,000 people), rather than wandering naturally.

Three main engineering structures built with public money and international loans – the Chashma Right Bank Canal, Taunsa Barrage, and marginal embankments – have collectively hemmed in the river, reducing its active width and altering sediment dynamics.

title: Smaller provinces?
author: none@none.com (Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry)
content:
AN intense debate on the need for smaller provinces has gripped the country. Is it a vote of no confidence in the current system, or the search for better governance? Let the facts speak. The UN’s Human Development Index places Pakistan in the low category, with persistent deprivation in health, education, and living standards. Over 88 million Pakistani citizens have no formal education. The infant mortality rate is 48 deaths per 1,000 live births against a global average of 18. Half the population lacks internet access. The current system may benefit some, but certainly not the majority of Pakistan’s 240m people. From this perspective, the current system of governance needs an overhaul. Pakistanis deserve good governance whether through smaller provinces or administrative units, or empowered local governments (LGs). The objective is to ensure public resources are used fairly, transparently, and in an accountable manner, and devolved to the lowest level of governance.
Defenders of the present system argue that the smaller provinces should only be created in accordance with constitutional provisions. This demand is valid. However, a question arises: why aren’t the provinces following another clear injunction of the same Constitution, ie, Article 140A, which directs them to set up empowered LG systems and devolve financial, political, and administrative authority for local development and services? If the provinces had strengthened grassroots democracy in the spirit of the Constitution, this debate would not have been necessary.
Status quo proponents claim to be the defenders of democracy, which is defined as a system of governance where power rests with the people, who exercise it through their elected representatives. If so, why aren’t provincial governments holding regular elections to establish LGs? Provincial finance commissions do not meet regularly. Instead, administrative authorities led by bureaucrats have been given LG functions. The current system lets provincial governments concentrate wealth in their own hands and keep it from reaching the grassroots, which runs counter to the essence of democracy.
The present system seems to be a victim of elite capture.
The present system seems to be a victim of elite capture, while ordinary folk suffer. The 18th Amendment devolved resources to the provinces, which refused to devolve them further to districts and tehsils. As a result, the quality of life for ordinary people in the far reaches of the provinces has not improved. The spirit of the 18th Amendment thus stands defeated. Provincial governments prefer megaprojects that devour resources at the expense of basic needs in the peripheries. MNAs and MPAs collect development funds to create their own patronage networks. This is not citizen-centric governance; it is elite capture.
It follows from all this that governance can improve only if the provinces or administrative units are manageable in size, and empowered LGs are made an integral part of the governance system. This is exactly the case in many well-governed countries. Italy has 110 provinces or administrative units that manage a population of 58.9m. So, the average population that each unit has to administer is a little over half a million. Japan has 47 prefectures, each of which administers an average of 2.6m people. The Netherlands has 12 provinces for a population of only 18m. Germany has 16 states or provinces to manage 83.5m people. Governance in all these countries is better because each citizen gets what he or she needs — right at the lowest level of administration.
Pakistanis rig- htly expect participatory governance mechanisms, with legal frameworks that apply fairly to all citizens. It is time Pakistan created reasonably sized administrative units through the appropriate constitutional amendment, preferably with consensus. Each unit should have an empowered LG that manages police, public safety infrastructure, water, sanitation, waste management, fire protection, education, parks, and libraries.
Several recommendations merit consideration. One, whenever parliament debates this issue, it must look more deeply into the political, constitutional, economic, and administrative aspects. Two, Article 140A of the Constitution should be amended to prohibit the arbitrary dissolution of LGs, ensure regular elections, guarantee fiscal devolution, and standardise LG functions and tenure in all the provinces. Three, Article 7 should explicitly include LGs as a separate tier in the overall state structure, with a share in the divisible pool of federal taxes. Four, MNAs’/ MPAs’ development funds should be reduced, but their power to oversee development work can be enhanced. 
The writer is a former foreign secretary. He currently serves as chairman of the Sanober Institute.
Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

title: Poverty’s long shadow
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S contribution to rising poverty across the Middle East, North Africa and the Afghanistan-Pakistan region is troubling.
According to the World Bank, the country accounts for nearly half of the region’s people living in extreme poverty. Ours is a story of repeated hardship. Millions of Pakistanis have endured the pandemic, deadly floods, soaring inflation, and years of economic uncertainty, often with little opportunity to recover before the next crisis arrives. For a poor household, each setback leaves lasting damage. Families may exhaust their savings, sell livestock, borrow money to buy food, or withdraw children from school to save expenses.
    
Even when prices stabilise and incomes improve, the losses are not easily reversed. A farmer who has sold his animals or a small trader who has closed his business cannot simply resume earning a livelihood. This helps explain why poverty can continue to rise even as the wider economy shows signs of recovery. The damage caused by successive crises has accumulated, leaving vulnerable families with fewer resources to withstand another blow.
Fresh dangers are emerging. The World Bank has warned that the conflict involving Iran could push up fuel and commodity prices, weaken remittances and increase borrowing costs. Adverse weather could also drive up food prices and hurt agricultural livelihoods. For households still struggling with the effects of earlier shocks, another spell of inflation could prove devastating. The government must, therefore, go beyond providing relief after disaster strikes. It needs to identify families at greatest risk, strengthen early-warning and disaster-response systems, protect farming livelihoods and ensure that financial help reaches vulnerable households before they are forced into desperate choices. Keeping children in school and preventing families from losing their means of earning a living must also be priorities. Poverty reduction cannot succeed if every new crisis pushes people back into hardship. Pakistan must protect the fragile gains its poorest citizens manage to make.

title: The lost civilian CT body
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
THIS is an obituary for the National Counter Terrorism Authority, once conceived as a civilian counterterrorism body that combined policymaking, coordination among law-enforcement agencies, and data collection and processing.
Since its inception in December 2008, and even after gaining legal cover under the Nacta Act, 2013, it has struggled to fully realise its role and mandate, while facing resistance from LEAs reluctant to coordinate with a police-led body.
Appointing a senior military officer as its national coordinator was not the first deviation from the Nacta Act. A bigger departure from the statute had come in 2025 with the establishment of the National Intelligence Fusion and Threat Assessment Centre. Niftac was created as a parallel body, apparently under Nacta but in effect superior to it, even though Nacta is the statutory body. This gave a superior security institution the leading role.
Nacta’s new form seems to have little to do with developing a counterterrorism strategy, building a coordination mechanism, or taking on a CT-related operational role. Its real purpose is to synchronise all civilian-led LEAs with the superior security institution, and, at the very least, to bring them under one roof. This synchronisation of internal security policy with the security doctrine conceived by the establishment’s top brass has been underway for a long time, taking various forms. Bureaucrats see it in the National Security and War Course (NSWC) at the National Defence University (NDU), which is now equivalent to the National Management Course, a mandatory course for promotion from Grade 20 to 21.
The NSWC gives senior bureaucrats more opportunities to align with evolving thinking at the top levels of the security institutions. At the narrative level, NDU and many other military-led institutions run short courses for opinion-makers, politicians, and business and community leaders to align them with the new thought process. Interestingly, all these courses and discourses happen at the expense of civilian governments, whether provincial or federal.
Nacta, the only civilian-led CT body, struggled to find its role and eventually lost.
One may argue that synchronisation within the internal security structure will improve coordination, the very dream for which Nacta was conceived. However, the new changes appear to be aimed at control, and the CT body is being used as an instrument of that. The structures of other LEAs, such as the police and FIA, leave little room for intervention by other institutions — unlike Nacta.
Admittedly, Nacta had a few good leaders who clearly understood the terrorism challenge facing the country and how to respond. But it is safe to say that most of its heads, and even others who served in the authority, had little idea of the CT body’s objectives. Many came on deputation, or to rest before landing a field posting.
    
As mentioned earlier, Nacta faced pressure and challenges from superior security institutions, which were reluctant to work under or with a civilian-led body. Still, the police cadre is undoubtedly responsible for destroying the institution and providing an excuse for its takeover. This did not happen overnight. The process began much earlier. When former prime minister Imran Khan chaired the Nacta board of governors meeting in September 2018, as required by law, two key realities emerged. One, he was the first prime minister to convene a board meeting since the Act was passed, even though quarterly meetings were required. Two, the national coordinator at the time recommended that the prime minister dissolve the body, as it had no use or role in countering terrorism in the country.
This was the first and last board meeting held under the original Act. In July 2019, parliament amended it through an ordinance, which it later passed in March 2020. The amendment made the interior minister the board chairman and the national coordinator its secretary. Several references to the “prime minister” in the Act were also replaced, shifting Nacta’s reporting line to the interior ministry. The 2019-2020 amendments thus downgraded Nacta from a prime minister-led federal-provincial body to one under the interior minister. Interestingly, one of the few board meetings held since then, and chaired by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, approved the establishment of Niftac. Just before Niftac was introduced, Nacta inducted around 130 permanent officers. Since Niftac’s establishment, most have struggled to find a role.
Niftac was described as a national platform connecting more than 50 federal and provincial departments and agencies — supported by provincial fusion centres — to improve intelligence coordination, speed up threat assessment, and strengthen information-sharing across institutional boundaries. That was Nacta’s purpose.
A military or intelligence institution can possess information that a civilian authority cannot access. It can conduct operations a civilian institution cannot. It can assess threats from a classified perspective. But the state also needs an institution that can sit openly with provincial police, civil administration, prosecutors, courts, parliamentarians, researchers and international partners. It needs an institution whose authority is intelligible within the civilian legal and administrative system.
Against this backdrop, Niftac overshadowed Nacta. Even before Maj Gen Faisal Naseer was appointed national coordinator, Niftac and its officers from the superior security institutions appeared more assertive and powerful than the national coordinator.
In fact, Nacta, the only civilian-led CT body, struggled to find its role and eventually lost that struggle. Now the vision and implementation plan will flow top-down, and space for consultation, policy discourse, and debate will gradually vanish.
This institutional transformation is taking place at a time when Pakistan faces its worst terrorism challenge, one that is growing more complex by the day. The state is trying hard to find a way out of the menace, but these transformations will not solve it. Concentrating power in one set of hands can be challenging because absolute control centralises the burden.
The writer is a security analyst.

title: Disturbing the peace
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THIS year’s Nobel Peace Prize is well-earned. The winner, South African jurist Dr Navi Pillay, has had an illustrious career defending human rights and speaking up for the oppressed globally. She worked as Nelson Mandela’s lawyer, served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, held the office of UN human rights chief, and was a judge at the International Criminal Court. Importantly, she headed a UN inquiry committee, which had the moral clarity to say that what Israel was doing in the occupied Gaza Strip amounted to genocide. This report was brave enough to assert what many self-proclaimed champions of human rights chose not to. The Nobel committee recognised Dr Pillay’s “efforts to promote peace and international law”. However, some are quite unhappy about this year’s choice. The American reaction, for example, has been petulant, bordering on the vicious. The US has sanctioned the ICC, with the secretary of state terming it a “rogue court”. President Donald Trump, who himself hoped to win this peace award, termed the decision “disgraceful and embarrassing” and an “indelible stain” on Norway, home of the Nobel Prize.
If anyone has been displaying rogue behaviour, it is the US. There may be many reasons for its hostility towards Dr Pillay and the ICC. For one, she has called out Israel for its genocidal violence, and defending Tel Aviv is seemingly a matter of faith for the US establishment. Secondly, Mr Trump’s reaction is incredibly petty. While the Nobel committee has given the peace prize to questionable recipients in the past, it is hard to fathom how Mr Trump — a leader who started a war of choice with Iran — could possibly qualify for a peace award. Even some of America’s closest allies — the European states and Japan — have been stunned by the ICC sanctions, and have expressed solidarity with the court. By sanctioning the ICC, the US has shown its contempt for international law and the global ‘rules-based order’. While this order is far from perfect, the US is looking to promote the law of the jungle globally, where America and its chosen allies can violate the rights of sovereign states at will, while their geopolitical enemies must bow in reverence. All free people of the world that believe in justice must resist this oppressive new normal.
Published in Dawn, October 11th, 2026

title: Arbitration and human rights
author: Muhammad Siddique Ali Pirzada
content:
Human rights and arbitration are often cast as opposing juridical worlds. One evokes public values, vulnerable claimants and state power; the other, contractual consent, private adjudication and commercial disputes. But that contrast obscures the question: when business activity causes human rights harm across borders, should effective remedy depend upon the institutional label of the forum? It should not. What matters is whether the mechanism can deliver legitimate, accessible and effective redress.

The European Law Institute's "Business and Human Rights: Access to Justice and Effective Remedies" Report presents a formidable objection. It calls the Bangladesh Accords and the Hague Rules on Business and Human Rights Arbitration "impressive and welcome", while cautioning that consensual mechanisms depend upon party consent and may be vulnerable to stronger parties without external control. It therefore favours public-facing mechanisms possessing coercive authority. That concern is legitimate. Yet it does not establish arbitration's irrelevance.

Indeed, the Report's treatment of contractual cascading points towards a more intriguing possibility. It proposes contractual mechanisms through which human-rights due-diligence responsibilities can extend through transnational supply chains, coupled with access to courts. If private ordering can carry substantive human rights responsibilities across borders, why should it become irrelevant when the question changes from who bears responsibility to how that responsibility may be contested and enforced? This does not displace courts; it asks that contractual responsibility and access to remedy be considered together.

That proposition encounters a fundamental limit: substantive obligation is not arbitral jurisdiction. An affected worker, community or other rightsholder does not acquire a right to arbitrate merely because two corporations have contracted. A credible model must address consent, standing, participation, applicable law and enforcement. Where appropriate, contractual arrangements may confer defined third-party rights and establish a legally cognisable basis for participation.

The Hague Rules address this problem at the procedural level. Based on the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules, they adapt procedure to business-and-human-rights disputes. Their framework can accommodate different claimant and respondent configurations, while consent remains its cornerstone. The Rules therefore do not create substantive rights or conjure jurisdiction where none exists; they demonstrate instead that arbitral procedure can be adapted beyond the conventional commercial paradigm.

Nor does the UN Guiding Principles framework reserve effective remedy to courts. It recognises judicial and non-judicial mechanisms and subjects non-state-based mechanisms to criteria including legitimacy, accessibility, predictability, equity, transparency and rights-compatibility. This is not an endorsement of arbitration as such. It is a functional standard against which arbitration must prove its worth.

That scrutiny must remain exacting. Arbitration cannot cure unequal bargaining power by invocation alone. Cost, evidentiary asymmetry, confidentiality, collective claims, third-party participation and enforcement may determine whether a formally available remedy is genuinely accessible. Courts remain indispensable where public coercive authority is required, consent is absent or mandatory law reserves the matter for judicial determination. An arbitration clause must never become a contractual alibi for extinguishing substantive rights or insulating corporate conduct from legitimate public oversight.

But these limitations establish the conditions of legitimate arbitration; they do not establish its irrelevance.

The better conception is neither courts versus arbitration nor private ordering versus public authority, but a plural remedial architecture in which institutional form follows remedial need. Courts possess coercive authority and public legitimacy that certain disputes require. Arbitration, where jurisdiction is validly constituted and safeguards exist, can offer a potentially neutral transnational forum, procedural adaptability and an enforceable determination.

Arbitration is no panacea. But excluding it from the remedial repertoire would be an untenable dogma.

While concerns about consensual mechanisms lacking external control are legitimate, arbitration's irrelevance is not established, as contractual arrangements can extend human rights responsibilities and potentially provide a basis for remedy.

Frameworks like the Hague Rules on Business and Human Rights Arbitration demonstrate how arbitral procedure can be adapted beyond conventional commercial paradigms to accommodate complex human rights disputes, building on UNCITRAL principles.

The article advocates for a plural remedial architecture where institutional form follows remedial need, recognizing the indispensable role of courts for coercive authority alongside arbitration's potential as a neutral, adaptable, and enforceable transnational forum.

title: Beneath the surface
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE IMF’s staff-level agreement with Pakistan on the fourth balance-of-payments and the third climate financing reviews came with little drama — which itself says something.
The mission spent two weeks in Islamabad, wrapped up the 2026 Article IV consultation, and left with a deal that releases $1.2bn once the IMF Executive Board approves it. Nobody expected a different outcome. The Fund is unlikely to push hard against a borrower that is hitting its fiscal targets. Compare this with March, when talks went virtual, ended without an agreement, and dragged on until the Board cleared funds in May. The recent round made fewer headlines because the hard bargaining over the budget had already been done. The current budget is built around a primary surplus of 2pc of GDP, and the lender is now collecting on that commitment. A programme that has settled into a routine reassures markets. It also shows how little room Islamabad has to depart from the script.
The lender’s own assessment is generous. It says the authorities have successfully navigated the fallout of the Middle East conflict and that policies have preserved stability. Reserves stand at about $21.5bn and inflation has eased from its May peak. Yet, a closer look shows that, at 10.3pc in September, inflation remains well above the State Bank’s medium-term target range. Last year’s growth of 3.6pc, with an annual population growth of nearly 2pc, leaves per capita gains thin.
The World Bank put poverty at about 42.4pc for 2025, and said growth was too weak to prevent an additional 1.9m people from slipping below the line in a single year. Exports tell the same story. Goods exports fell about 6pc to $30.1bn, of which textiles accounted for $17.9bn. Imports rose 8pc to $69.8bn, widening the merchandise trade deficit to $39.6bn. Growth in IT services kept total exports near $40bn, which though welcome, is no substitute for a manufacturing base that sells more abroad.
The recommendations deserve more attention than the headline figure. The lender wants the fuel support scheme phased out, calling it costly and too broadly targeted. Unwinding a broad subsidy is politically harder than agreeing to end it on paper. It also wants timely tariff adjustments so that the circular debt does not return, a medium-term tax strategy, private participation in power distribution, better governance of SOEs, and progress on privatisation. Many who have read the earlier review statements will recognise the list. When the same agenda is repeated, the question one must ask is: how much has changed? The Fund’s language of commitment does not answer it. The tranche will arrive. What the government has yet to demonstrate is an economy that grows fast enough to cut poverty and sells more abroad — an issue that cannot be put off much longer.
Published in Dawn, October 9th, 2026

title: Legal remedies
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
THE missing persons’ issue is not new. The post-Soviet political tumult in the world released the pent-up energy of ethnic and ideological conflicts that had lain dormant under the stabilising hold of totalitarianism.
Consequently, as armed conflicts amongst and within nations intensified, the number of missing persons remained high during the mid-1990s. An international commission for missing persons was established in 1996 to track and resolve the issue in Yugoslavia’s conflict. The commission’s mandate was expanded in 2003 to include the global issues of missing persons in various conflicts, natural disasters, and climate migrations. 
The International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance was signed in 2006, which defined enforced disappearance as “the arrest, detention, abduction or any other form of deprivation of liberty by agents of the state or by persons or groups of persons acting with the authorisation, support or acquiescence of the state”. The treaty entered into force in 2010.
The missing persons issue got further traction with the rise of ideologically inspired waves of terrorism by organisations like Al Qaeda, IS and several others. UNSC resolutions 1267, 1998, and 2253 established a list of terrorist entities including Al Qaeda, the Taliban, and IS to sanction these along with their financiers. Despite these international efforts, the domestic legal options to deal with terrorist entities remained fragmented. As a consequence, the issue of missing persons was conflated with the issue of enforced disappearances. 
Our low terrorism prosecution rate signals dysfunction.
It is difficult to separate voluntary and enforced disappearances globally. In Pakistan, a Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances was established in 2011 which has dealt with 10,947 missing persons’ cases throughout Pakistan and has resolved 9,447 (86 per cent) cases.
When judicial prosecution of hardened criminals becomes ineffective, it can create incentives for law-enforcement agencies to resort to vigilante justice. This can further create space for allegations of enforced disappearances where apprehension of terrorism suspects is not immediately followed by prosecution. Due care needs to be taken to sift cases of voluntary disappearances, crime-related arrests, and terrorism-related detentions. Differential legal treatment and prosecution are required to avoid a predilection for non-legal remedies on the part of LEAs. Pakistan’s low terrorism prosecution rate (8pc) over the past two decades, compared with 88pc in the UK, 99pc in China and 99.9pc in Japan, signals a dysfunctional prosecution system.
The inordinate delays in prosecution and conviction of terrorists create space for their political supporters to exploit legal gaps and build victimhood narratives. In Balochistan, terrorist organisations have spawned a fear psychosis by abducting judges in order to stymie the prosecution process. A few examples include the assassination of justice Muhammad Noor Mesk­anzai, former chief justice of Balochistan High Court in Kharan in 2022, and killing of district and sessions judge Abdul Hakeem Kaka in Mastung in July 2026. 
The threat extends beyond judges, with around 50 CTD officials killed in Balochistan, while the driver of a law officer was shot when the officer was recording his statement concerning the July 2026 Ziarat terrorist attack in which 27 policemen were killed.
To tackle these challenges, the government has amended Pakistan’s Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) 1997 thro­u­gh the insertion of Section 11-EEEE that provides for ‘Prev­e­ntive Dete­ntion for Inquiry’, allowing detention for up to 90 days for inquiry, thereby pro­viding a legal mechanism for investigating terrorism suspects by collecting evidence before moving to prosecute them. 
The Anti-Terrorism (Balochistan Amendment) Act, 2025, incorporates the amended ATA, 1997, to the province, enabling LEAs and the judiciary to detain the accused for 90 days, while Section 21-AAA of the Anti-Terrorism (Punjab Amendment) Act, 2026, provides protection to judges and witnesses.
Since the implementation of the new law in Balochistan, out of 90 detainees, five have been released where the allegations could not be established, while 40 have been referred for trial through faceless courts, demonstrating movement from preventive detention towards prosecution through a defined legal process.
All the above measures show the government’s resolve to extend the full range of legal remedies to LEAs and the judiciary to arrest, investigate, and prosecute the terrorists, with celerity, and in accordance with the law, bringing much-needed transparency and fairness to the whole process. 
The writer has a PhD from Nust.
